options.misconception: assumes remittances are always taxed away

options.text: They influence only consumption in the homeland, never who wins elections there
options.misconception: confuses economic effect with political effect

questions.explanation: Transfers can fund parties and campaigns in the homeland, so money sent by diaspora families carries political weight. Treating them as purely private overlooks this channel.
questions.hint: Ask what the funds can be spent on.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the gap to a majority determines what a government can do
questions.stem: Margin comment: the translator must explain in a note how a government's distance from a legislative majority should be characterised.

answer.exemplar: The gap between a government's seats and the threshold for a working majority determines how much it must persuade to legislate. A government holding 54 of 100 seats in a chamber where 60 are needed faces a blocking minority of six, so its options are negotiation and budget measures rather than command, and the note should say so plainly rather than describing the situation as stable or unstable in the abstract.

questions.explanation: The distance to a threshold tells the reader whether a government can command or must bargain. Describing the position as stable or unstable hides the number that matters.
questions.hint: Ask how many votes are still missing.

options.misconception: ignores home language in explaining results

options.text: The gap proves the testing language is unlawful, since no language should be used for examinations
options.misconception: treats a measured gap as a legal verdict

questions.explanation: A test in the language of instruction measures performance in that language, so lower reading scores may reflect the language of teaching rather than weaker reading. Legal conclusions do not follow.
questions.hint: Ask what the test actually measures.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the direction of causation between transfers and political preference

stimulus.body: Households receiving transfers tend to support the parties that campaigned on diaspora issues during the last election, and local associations built by earlier migrants now lobby on the homeland's behalf. options.text: Transfers are shaped by exchange rates and settlement patterns, so political preference may follow the money
options.misconception: treats transfers as purely economic

options.text: Transfers buy votes directly, and the political preferences of recipients follow the funds
options.misconception: assumes money buys settled political allegiance

options.text: The flow of transfers may reflect political alignment, and the direction of causation is unclear
Only long-established migrants receive transfers, so early arrivals remain politically outside
options.misconception: confuses earliest arrivals with later migrants

questions.explanation: The passage raises causation in both directions: preferences may shape where money goes, and money may then buy influence. Flows also respond to economics, so the pattern need not run one way.
questions.hint: Ask which way the causal arrow points.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why universally shared obligations support the state's claim to allegiance
questions.stem: Query for the author: the translator must explain why shared institutions are thought to bind a state together.

answer.exemplar: Shared institutions create obligations that run across the whole population: conscription pools, common courts, a single currency of account and joint disaster response all require the state to act for people it has no special reason to favour. Because participation is universal and its benefits are shared, the institutions give the state a claim on allegiance that is harder to question than the claim of any single group, and they make the cost of leaving visible to everyone.

questions.explanation: Universally shared obligations give the state a claim on allegiance that special-interest bargains cannot match. Their value lies in applying impartially across the whole population.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the obligation general.

options.text: The draft sentence is supported, because a higher grant rate always reflects fairer criteria

questions.explanation: The passage attributes much of the rise to the test format while noting other factors, so the sentence must not claim the reform produced the whole rise. Co-movement proves no cause.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Computing a group's share of residents
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a group's share of residents is calculated and read
questions.stem: Editorial annotation: the translator must explain to readers how a group's share of residents should be calculated and read.

answer.exemplar: A group's share of residents is the number of people in the group divided by the total resident population of the area in question, expressed as a percentage, and the denominator must be the whole population rather than a subset. The choice of denominator changes the answer, so a figure of 15 per cent of all residents may be 40 per cent of recent arrivals. Comparisons also require the same boundaries and the same reference year, otherwise a rising share may reflect newcomers arriving in a shrinking district rather than any change in the group's circumstances.

questions.explanation: The denominator determines the share, so the same group can be a small fraction of residents and a large fraction of newcomers. Comparisons need matching boundaries and reference years.
questions.hint: Ask what the denominator includes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why institutional confidence indicates belonging
questions.stem: Explanatory note: the translator must explain why confidence in public institutions is treated as evidence of belonging.

answer.exemplar: Institutional confidence measures whether people expect the state to act reliably on their behalf, and that expectation is what makes settlement durable. Someone who believes that complaints are answered, services maintained and rules applied alike can plan a life there, while someone who expects indifference plans to leave. Belonging is therefore not only an emotional attitude but a practical calculation about whether the political community will hold still for you.

questions.explanation: Belonging shows up in whether people expect the state to act reliably toward them, which makes the idea operational rather than sentimental. Reliable institutions give reasons to stay.
questions.hint: Ask what people expect institutions to do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why arguments for restricting membership generate their own injustice
questions.stem: Explanatory box: the translator must explain to readers why arguments about restricting membership are contested.

answer.exemplar: Restricting membership is contested because the arguments for it pull against the principles it is supposed to defend. An economic argument says citizens must not be asked to subsidise services for people who contribute nothing, yet every restriction also excludes families who do contribute, and the line is hard to draw without becoming discriminatory. A cultural argument says a state must preserve a shared way of life, yet it defines who belongs by characteristics that cannot be applied evenly. Both arguments therefore generate their own injustice, which is why every scheme is contested.

questions.explanation: Arguments for restriction tend to generate the harms they claim to prevent, since drawing the line protects some and excludes others arbitrarily. That tension is why every scheme is contested.
questions.hint: Ask what each justification excludes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Check a gloss on competing grounds of legitimacy against its source

stimulus.body: Consent grounds the state's authority in the will of the governed; self-determination grounds a territorial claim in the will of the people of a territory. The two can pull apart: a government may command wide consent within its borders while a minority population claims the right to secede, and commentators dispute whether the second claim is grounded in consent to the state or is a ground against it.

questions.stem: Note for the proofreader: the translator is checking a gloss on the two grounds of legitimacy against the source passage.

options.text: The gloss is accurate, because consent and self-determination both rest on the will of a people
options.misconception: collapses two distinct grounds into one

options.text: The gloss is accurate, because self-determination always defeats a consent-based state
options.misconception: makes self-determination always override consent

options.text: The gloss is wrong, because the passage says self-determination has no connection to consent
options.misconception: denies any connection the passage draws

options.text: The gloss should note that the two grounds can conflict over a minority's claim to secede

questions.explanation: The passage stresses that the two grounds can pull apart where a minority claims the right to secede, which a gloss omitting that conflict would miss. The passage does not settle their priority.
questions.hint: Ask where the two grounds conflict.

answer.exemplar: What lets a government govern is not the number of parties it contains but the number of votes it can deliver as one block, because a legislature passes or blocks legislation by division. answer.exemplar: Transfers are politically significant because money moved by a community abroad becomes resources used at home: funding party campaigns, paying for community organisations, sustaining schools and religious institutions, and financing visits by homeland politicians. questions.learningObjective: Explain why test scores can mislead about learning
questions.stem: Background note: the translator must explain to readers why test results can mislead about how well children are learning.

answer.exemplar: A test administered in a language a pupil does not use at home measures two things at once: what the child knows and how fluently the child operates in the language of the exam. Where the language of instruction and the language of assessment differ, the second element depresses the score, so the ranking of pupils reflects language familiarity as much as subject mastery. Reading the same pupils' oral answers, or testing in their strongest language, separates the two and often shows a gap between measured ranking and actual learning.

questions.explanation: A test in a second language blends subject knowledge with unfamiliarity in that language, so scores rank language familiarity alongside learning. Comparing oral work separates the two.

answer.exemplar: The grant rate divides the number of applications granted by the number of applications decided in the same period, and it says nothing about those still pending. Because the rate conditions on reaching a decision, a backlog can flatter it: a person whose file sits unresolved is excluded from both the numerator and the denominator, so a high rate may simply describe an administration that processes easy cases quickly and leaves difficult ones open. Read with the refusal reasons, the rate becomes informative; read alone, it is a headline.

questions.explanation: The rate excludes pending files, so it describes throughput on decided cases, not the whole caseload. Read with refusal reasons it is informative; alone it flatters the administration.
questions.hint: Ask which cases the denominator contains.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the term diaspora carries two opposed senses
questions.stem: Terminology guidance: the translator must explain to readers why the word diaspora carries a tension rather than one settled meaning.

answer.exemplar: The word diaspora is used in two ways that pull against each other: to describe a dispersed people whose members feel a tie to a homeland, and to describe the territory they were dispersed from as something already settled by others. The first sense is about connection and often carries a claim to collective entitlement; the second is about a historical fact of settlement and carries no such claim. A translation that fixes on either sense alone will misrepresent the politics that use the word, since homeland governments and diaspora organisations draw on the two meanings for opposing purposes.

questions.explanation: The term carries a tension between a claim of connection to a homeland and a description of a place settled by others. Fixing on one sense distorts the politics built on both.
questions.hint: Ask which two usages the word serves.

questions.learningObjective: Check a glossary definition against its source passage

stimulus.body: A claim to state legitimacy may rest on consent, meaning that authority is exercised with the agreement of the governed, or on self-determination, meaning that a people is entitled to determine its political allegiance. The two grounds answer different questions, and a government may satisfy the first for the territory as a whole while a territorial minority invokes the second against it.

questions.stem: Closing note for the reader: the translator needs a gloss for state legitimacy and has attached the passage it comes from.

options.text: State legitimacy means the consent of the governed, with self-determination as one way of evidencing it
options.misconception: collapses two grounds into a single definition

options.text: State legitimacy means self-determination, since consent alone cannot justify rule
options.misconception: makes consent irrelevant to legitimacy

options.text: State legitimacy concerns only the borders of the state, since consent is a separate question
options.misconception: confines legitimacy to territorial questions

options.text: State legitimacy concerns whether political authority is justified, and two distinct grounds are recognised

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes two grounds of legitimacy answering different questions, so a gloss should present them as alternatives within justified authority. Collapsing them misdescribes it.
questions.hint: Ask how many grounds the passage names.
